title: Quarks, leptons and the classification of particles

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: The fundamental particles of the standard picture at AS level: the six quark flavours, their charges and antiquarks, the quark composition of the proton and the neutron, hadrons as baryons and mesons, the quark changes in β-decay, and the leptons.

blocks.heading: Fundamental particles and the six quark flavours
blocks.text: A fundamental particle is one with no smaller constituents: there is nothing inside it to take apart, no experiment that splits it into something else. Quarks are fundamental, and there are six flavours (types) of them: up, down, strange, charm, top and bottom. The word flavour means nothing more exotic than type - it is the physicist's word for which of the six a quark is, the way a shop might speak of six flavours of the same kind of sweet. The up and down quarks are the pair that matter every day, because they make the proton and the neutron, and so every atom of every substance; the other four flavours appear in heavier, short-lived particles produced in high-energy collisions, and at this level they are met and named rather than used. The idea of a fundamental particle is the classification that drives this whole section, so it is worth being exact about it. A particle either has smaller constituents or it does not, and that single question sorts everything that follows. Protons and neutrons do have constituents - quarks - so they are not fundamental, whatever their everyday fame. Quarks and leptons do not, so they are, as far as any experiment has ever shown.

blocks.heading: The charge of each quark flavour
blocks.text: The charge of a quark is a fraction of the elementary charge e. The up, charm and top quarks each carry +⅔e. The down, strange and bottom quarks each carry −⅓e. A handy grouping keeps them apart: the quarks whose names point up (up, charm, top) carry +⅔e, and the rest (down, strange, bottom) carry −⅓e. Each antiquark carries the opposite charge to its quark: anti-up is −⅔e, anti-down is +⅓e, anti-charm is −⅔e, anti-strange is +⅓e, anti-top is −⅔e and anti-bottom is +⅓e. No knowledge of any other property of quarks is needed at this level: charge is the one number the syllabus asks you to recall and use, and the two fractions above are all of it. Notice what the fractions make possible. Two thirds and one third add to one: ⅔e + ⅓e = +1e, and ⅔e − ⅓e − ⅓e = 0. Whole charges come from combining the fractions, which is exactly how the proton gets its +1e and the neutron its zero, as the next block shows.

blocks.heading: Protons and neutrons are made of quarks
blocks.text: Protons and neutrons are not fundamental particles, because each is made of quarks. A proton holds two up quarks and one down quark, written uud. A neutron holds one up quark and two down quarks, written udd. Check the compositions against the charges and they confirm themselves. A proton's quarks carry +⅔e + ⅔e − ⅓e, which adds to +1e, the charge a proton is measured with. A neutron's carry +⅔e − ⅓e − ⅓e, which adds to 0, the charge a neutron is measured with. The charge arithmetic is the reason these compositions and not others: three up quarks would give +2e and three down quarks −1e, and neither is a particle you will meet as a proton or a neutron. So the names of the quarks inside each nucleon can be recovered from the charge alone, if you remember that each is three quarks: a total of +1e from three thirds needs two ups and a down, and a total of 0 needs one up and two downs.

blocks.heading: Hadrons: baryons and mesons
blocks.text: A hadron is a particle made of quarks, and every hadron is either a baryon or a meson. A baryon consists of three quarks: the proton (uud) and the neutron (udd) are the two baryons you meet every day, and every baryon you are asked about is three quarks, no more and no fewer. A meson consists of one quark and one antiquark, so it holds two constituents, not three, and its quark and antiquark need not share a flavour: an up quark paired with an anti-down antiquark is a meson, and so is a strange quark paired with an anti-up antiquark - the classification asks how many and which kind of constituents, not whether they match. The classification is a two-way sort with no third box: three quarks makes a baryon, a quark and an antiquark makes a meson, and anything made of quarks is one or the other. The proton and the neutron, being made of quarks, are hadrons; being made of three quarks, they are baryons. Learn the chain in one line: made of quarks means hadron; three quarks means baryon; one quark and one antiquark means meson.

blocks.heading: Worked example: a meson's charge
blocks.text: A meson is built from an up quark and an anti-down antiquark. What charge does it carry? Add the constituents' charges: the up quark carries +⅔e and the anti-down antiquark carries +⅓e, so the meson carries ⅔e + ⅓e = +1e. The two fractions add to a whole elementary charge, which is typical of quark combinations: quark charges come in thirds, and combinations of quarks and antiquarks add to whole multiples of e. Test the rule the other way before trusting it. Had the pairing been an up quark with a plain down quark, the total would be ⅔e − ⅓e = +⅓e, which is not a whole charge - and that pairing is not a meson anyway, because a meson needs one quark and one antiquark, not two quarks. The charge arithmetic and the classification rule work together: one tells you what the particle is worth, the other tells you what it is, and a candidate answer that breaks either is wrong.

blocks.heading: Quark changes in β-decay
blocks.text: β-decay, described in section 11.1 as the emission of an electron or a positron together with an (anti)neutrino, is at quark level a change inside one nucleon of the nucleus. In β⁻-decay a down quark becomes an up quark, so a neutron (udd) becomes a proton (uud); in β⁺-decay an up quark becomes a down quark, so a proton (uud) becomes a neutron (udd). The direction follows the decay: β⁻-decay leaves the nucleus with one more proton and the same nucleon number, which means a neutron must have become a proton, which means a down quark became an up quark; β⁺-decay is the exact reverse. The charges confirm the direction, so the rule can be re-derived from the charge books rather than remembered. In β⁻-decay the quark change is −⅓e → +⅔e, a rise of 1e, and the emitted β⁻-particle's charge of −1e balances it, keeping the total charge the same before and after. In β⁺-decay the change is +⅔e → −⅓e, a fall of 1e, and the emitted positron's +1e balances that. Reverse the quark change by accident and the emitted particle comes out wrong too: the conservation books of section 11.1 and the quark charges agree, or the equation is not β-decay.

blocks.heading: Leptons
blocks.text: Electrons and neutrinos are fundamental particles called leptons: they are not made of quarks, and nothing smaller has ever been found inside them. The lepton family in this topic holds the electron, the positron, the neutrino and the antineutrino - the positron being the electron's antiparticle and the antineutrino the neutrino's. The β-particles and (anti)neutrinos a nucleus emits in β-decay are leptons, not hadrons, whatever their origin in a nuclear process: where a particle comes from does not change what it is. The split between hadrons and leptons is the top-level sort of the standard picture: hadrons are made of quarks, leptons are fundamental and not made of quarks, and a particle is one or the other, never both and never neither. A proton is a hadron and a baryon; an electron is a lepton; a neutrino is a lepton; a neutron is a hadron and a baryon. Nothing that decays in this topic crosses the line, which is what makes the classification stable enough to test.

blocks.heading: The errors the classification catches
blocks.text: Three errors account for most lost marks here. Giving a meson three quarks: a meson is one quark and one antiquark, two constituents, and assuming the pair shares a flavour is a second error on the same card. Calling the proton or the neutron fundamental: both are baryons made of three quarks, and only quarks and leptons are fundamental in this topic. Giving a quark the wrong charge: up, charm and top carry +⅔e; down, strange and bottom carry −⅓e; and the antiquarks carry the opposites. Each error is caught by one test: count the constituents (two or three?), ask whether it has smaller parts, and check the fraction of e against the flavour.

blocks.heading: Why the standard picture is a classification, not a zoo
blocks.text: The particle names in this topic are few, and the classification does the work of remembering them. Start from the top question: is the particle made of quarks? If yes, it is a hadron, and the next question is how many constituents: three quarks makes it a baryon, and one quark plus one antiquark makes it a meson. If no, it is a lepton, and the leptons in this topic are the electron, the positron, the neutrino and the antineutrino, all fundamental. Under the baryons sit the proton (uud) and the neutron (udd), the two you already use; every other name in the classification is a box, and the boxes are what the syllabus asks about. The sort runs in one direction only, so every particle lands in exactly one box, and no particle is both fundamental and made of quarks - which is what makes the classification safe to test.

blocks.heading: Worked example: checking a stated composition
blocks.text: A revision card claims that a baryon with quark composition uds... take a cleaner case. A learner writes that the neutron is uud and the proton udd, the wrong way round. Check each against its charge. The learner's neutron (uud) would carry ⅔e + ⅔e − ⅓e = +1e, but a neutron is measured with zero charge, so the composition fails; the learner's proton (udd) would carry ⅔e − ⅓e − ⅓e = 0, but a proton is measured with +1e. Both fail, and swapping them back fixes both: neutron udd, proton uud. The check is mechanical - add the thirds, compare with the measured charge - and it works for any three-quark composition you are asked to test.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The quark picture completes the account of β-decay from section 11.1: the emitted electron and antineutrino of a β⁻-decay are leptons, and the change that released them was a down quark becoming an up quark inside one nucleon. The charges of the up and down quarks are the arithmetic behind the conservation of charge: adding ⅔e, ⅔e and −⅓e is the same bookkeeping as balancing the proton numbers across a decay equation. The elementary charge e itself was met in topic 9 as the size of the charge on an electron, and it is the same e every quark charge is a fraction of. The classification habit - fundamental or not, hadron or lepton, baryon or meson - is the sort of sorting that topic 1's quantity language makes precise, and the same habit of asking what is inside what organises the whole of the physical world this syllabus walks through.
